The derivation begins with the fundamental physics of radar reception, where the desired echo signal competes against thermal noise and exogenous RF interference. Mathematically, we define the instantaneous Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio (SINR) as the primary state variable. When interference power approaches the receiver's dynamic range limits, the system undergoes a bifurcation from linear amplification to non-linear saturation. This physical degradation is abstracted into the `radar_snr_degradation` primitive, serving as a universal operator for any sensing apparatus subjected to hostile or chaotic environments. Concurrently, the mitigation of such degradation relies on distributed sensing, captured by the `multi_source_coop_matrix`. By aggregating independent observations from diverse agencies (FAA, Coast Guard, etc.), the effective Fisher Information increases, reducing the Cramér-Rao lower bound on estimation error. In the context of Galaxy Sports Intelligence, these primitives map directly to the challenges of tracking athletes through visual occlusions or sensor dropout. The interference operator models the sudden loss of tracking fidelity, while the cooperative matrix represents the Bayesian fusion of disparate data sources—such as computer vision, GPS, and biomechanical sensors—to reconstruct the true kinematic state. The duality lies in the tension between localized vulnerability (receiver saturation) and global resilience (cooperative averaging). Failure modes emerge when the interference is correlated across all sensors, breaking the independence assumption of the cooperative matrix and leading to catastrophic state estimation collapse.
